Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on what I have done wrong
I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
I can't deal with even the slightest upset
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

vignette:
Kwame had never liked bars much, but that night a friend had dragged him out to celebrate a promotion. The streets were loud, and the air carried a mix of cheap beer and cologne. He didn't remember exactly how it started-just a figure stepping out of a doorway, a voice demanding his wallet. He remembered the smell, warm and sour, and then a heavy object-a bottle?-striking his shoulder before he could react. The man's face twisted with anger, shouting words Kwame's brain didn't process. After that, only a handful of moments stayed with him: the asphalt against his cheek, the screech of a car, a pair of boots landing nearby. Then nothing.

Those moments had become snapshots, frozen images that came without warning. He would be sitting at his desk in the municipal planning office, reviewing zoning maps, and suddenly he saw the fragment of a gray sidewalk, a broken piece of glass. The emotion hit him so fast and so hard that he had to drop everything-push back his chair, press his palms against his thighs, wait for the wave to pass. His heart pounded. Sometimes his breath got stuck. When his supervisor asked what was wrong, Kwame could only shake his head. He knew the story: the assault, the police report that went nowhere, the officer who said there was little to go on. But he could not find the words to describe what he actually felt. The pieces wouldn't line up in his mouth.

In the months afterward, he started to avoid anything that felt like confrontation. At work, when a colleague pushed back on a traffic-flow proposal, Kwame would nod quickly and say nothing, even if he disagreed. He took on solo projects, stayed quiet in meetings. Any expression of anger-even a raised eyebrow or a firm tone-sent a chill through his chest. Once, a coworker slammed a drawer shut and Kwame flinched so visibly that the person apologized. Part of him believed that if he stopped an argument from starting, he could stop something worse. He could not trust safety. Even when his boss assured him the office was a good environment, Kwame felt like something bad was always about to happen.

The smell of alcohol became unbearable. Passing a bar on his walk home, he would cross the street, sometimes walking six blocks out of his way. If a colleague returned from lunch with beer on his breath, Kwame would invent a reason to leave the room. He knew he was overreacting, but the smell seemed to pull him straight back to that doorway, to the sour heat of a stranger's rage.

At night he could not stop turning the assault over in his head. He dwelled on what he had done wrong: Why hadn't he just handed over his wallet immediately? Why had he argued back? Why had he walked down that street at all? He told himself he was stupid, irresponsible, weak. And then, to quiet the spiral, he started gambling. Small bets at first-online poker, sports pools. The rush of a win replaced the hollow feeling for an hour or two. He lost more than he won, but the distraction worked. On bad nights he would stay up until 3 a.m. chasing that numbness.

Everyday sounds set him off. The slam of a car door. A dropped clipboard. A sudden laugh in the hallway. His body reacted before his mind caught up-a violent jump, shoulders tensed, pulse racing. Unexpected movements, even harmless ones like someone reaching for a stapler, made him feel as though he were under attack. He knew rationally that he was safe. He could hear himself repeat the reassurance. But it did not stick. The terror came from somewhere deeper, and he had no authority over it.

What had finally brought Kwame to the clinic was a moment in a weekly planning meeting. A senior planner, frustrated with a budget delay, tossed a pen across the table. It clattered and bounced. Kwame gasped, stood up, and walked out without a word. He sat in the bathroom stall for twenty minutes, shaking, convinced he could not handle anything. The institution he had trusted-the police, his own office-had not protected him before, and he saw no reason to believe they would now. He felt helpless. Even a tiny upset felt like collapse.

Now he sat across from the intake worker, trying to put all of this into a sentence. He managed to say he was afraid of losing his job. But what he really wanted, what he could not yet express aloud, was to find a way to believe that the next ordinary sound, the next raised voice, the next whiff of alcohol, would not destroy him again.
